手搖琴前身可能源自歐洲或中東提琴，公元11世紀前已見。9世紀波斯地理學家 Ibn: The hurdy-gurdy may descend from the European or Middle Eastern fiddle, and it is found before the eleventh century. The ninth-century Persian geographer Ibn Khurradadhbih described the Byzantine lira; tenth-century Arabic texts mention a similar instrument as well. The early organistrum was large and needed two people to work it; it was tuned in Pythagorean fifths and used for singing in church. In the thirteenth century it shrank into the one-person symphonia, with the keys pressed from below, which suits fast tunes. It was popular in the Renaissance, when the buzzing bridge appeared. At the end of the seventeenth century it sank for a while into a lower-class instrument, then in the eighteenth century came back into polite society with French rococo taste, developing into the six-string vielle à roue and passing into Central Europe and Ukraine. By the early twentieth century many forms had died out; it drew attention again through the folk revival and through a mention in a 1968 pop song.
手搖琴屬弦鳴樂器，見於歐洲、中東、亞洲與全球民間音樂。發聲體為琴弦，來源提及旋律: The hurdy-gurdy is a chordophone found in the folk music of Europe, the Middle East, Asia and the wider world. The sounding body is the strings; sources mention melody strings and drone strings, and gut strings. The wheel is coated with resin and sounds the strings by friction. The keys are wooden or metal wedge-shaped tangents that press the strings to change pitch. The soundboard and the hollow body make the vibration of the strings audible. Sources do not state the materials of the body, the bridge, the handle and the other parts.
手搖琴常見於法國、奧克西塔尼亞、阿拉貢、卡津、阿斯圖里亞斯、坎塔布里亞、加利西亞: The hurdy-gurdy is common in the folk music of France, Occitania, Aragon, Cajun Louisiana, Asturias, Cantabria, Galicia, Hungary and the Slavic lands, and it is also used in medieval, Renaissance and early Baroque music, often alternating with the bagpipes or playing alongside them. Blind travelling musicians in Ukraine used it for quasi-religious repertoire, epic songs and folk dances. In eighteenth-century French aristocratic circles there was Nicolas Chédeville's Il pastor Fido; the last song of Schubert's Winterreise portrays a street musician playing it, and Donovan's pop song "Hurdy Gurdy Man" stirred interest by naming the instrument in its lyric.

The hurdy-gurdy is a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 321.321-72. The player turns a handle, which drives a resined wheel inside the body against the strings; the melody is made by keys pushing tangents onto the strings to change pitch. The body has a soundboard and a resonating cavity, and most instruments carry drone strings that give a bagpipe-like continuous note, while a drone string (trompette) and the buzzing bridge (chien) can produce a percussive buzz. It is found in Europe, the Middle East, Asia and around the world, and is common in French, Occitan, Aragonese, Cajun French, Asturian, Cantabrian, Galician, Hungarian and Slavic folk music; it also appears in medieval, Renaissance and early Baroque settings, often alternating with the bagpipes or paired with them, and in Ukraine it is found among blind street musicians as well.
手搖琴的基本操作順序是：一手穩定轉動手柄，帶動腹腔內樹脂輪摩擦琴弦；另一手操作鍵: The basic order of playing the hurdy-gurdy is this: one hand turns the handle steadily, driving the resined wheel inside the body against the strings; the other works the keyboard, so that wooden or metal tangents press the melody strings and change the pitch. Begin by keeping the wheel turning evenly, then add the keys, so that the melody string and several drone strings sound at once and make a continuous bass. If the instrument has a highest drone string, it can be led over the buzzing bridge; as the wheel speeds up, the foot of the bridge vibrates and gives a percussive buzz. Early large models needed two people, one turning the crank and one pressing the keys; later ones let a single player turn the wheel and work keys pressed from below at the same time.
手搖琴的音色具有獨特的溫潤而略帶蒼涼的質感，音調沉穩而富有神祕感。其音域跨度廣闊: The hurdy-gurdy has a particular timbre, warm and a little desolate, steady in pitch and full of mystery. Its range is wide, from a deep fundamental to a clear high register, but the low and middle range is the fullest and strongest. Because the strings vibrate without pause under the resined wheel, the resonance is even and long, sustained and continuous like a bowed violin, with an old-fashioned elegance on top. Against the bright penetration of a violin, the hurdy-gurdy sounds heavier and more brooding; beside an organ, it has more human warmth and expression. This particular character makes it easy to recognise, and it often sets a mood of dream, nostalgia or folk life.
